concept.technique_name: geometric progression of square sides via diagonal relation

examples.problem_statement: Let S_1, S_2, .... be the squares such that for each n \ge 1, the length of the diagonal of S_n is equal to the length of the side of S_{n+1}. If the length of the side of S_3 is 4 cm. What is the area of the square S_{11}?

solution.description: Apply the rule given in the problem to the pair S_2, S_3: the side of S_3 equals the diagonal of S_2, so the diagonal of S_2 is 4 cm.
Convert the diagonal back to a side: a square's side is 1/\sqrt{2} times its diagonal, so divide 4 by \sqrt{2} to get the side of S_2.
Repeat the same divide-by-\sqrt{2} move one step further back to get the side of S_1 from the side of S_2.

solution.result: \text{sides form a GP with common ratio } \sqrt{2}
solution.description: Compare the three sides just found and notice each is \sqrt{2} times the previous one, so the consecutive sides form a geometric progression of ratio \sqrt{2}.
Write the general term of that GP from first term 2 and ratio \sqrt{2}, then collect the powers of 2 into the single exponent (n+1)/2.
Substitute n = 11 into the general term to get the side length of the eleventh square.
Square the side length just obtained, since the area of a square is the side squared.

key_reminders: The side of a square is 1/\sqrt{2} times its diagonal (equivalently, diagonal = side \times \sqrt{2}).
A sequence whose each term is a fixed multiple of the previous one is a GP: n-th term = first term \times r^{\,n-1}.
common_mistakes: Indexing off by one: the side of S_3 is the diagonal of S_2, not of S_3, so the chain steps backwards from n = 3.
Multiplying by \sqrt{2} instead of dividing when going from a diagonal down to the side of the smaller square.
Reporting the side 64 cm as the answer instead of squaring it to get the area.

concept.technique_name: closure of integers under arithmetic operations

examples.problem_statement: Which of the following must produce integers? Indicate all such statements. (A) Integer \times Integer (B) Integer \div Integer (C) Integer + Integer (D) Integer - Integer (E) Prime \times Prime (F) Prime \div Prime

solution.description: Check the three closed operations first: multiplying, adding, or subtracting one integer with another always lands back on an integer, so (A), (C) and (D) are in.
Test division separately: the outcome depends on the particular values of the two integers, so (B) may fail to produce an integer.
Note that primes are themselves integers, so multiplying two primes obeys the same closure rule established in step 1 and (E) must produce an integer.
Apply the one exception for primes: dividing a prime by a different prime can never give an integer; only a prime divided by itself, e.g. 3 \div 3 = 1, does, so (F) is not guaranteed.

examples.answer: (A) Integer × Integer; (C) Integer + Integer; (D) Integer − Integer;

key_reminders: The integers are closed under multiplication, addition and subtraction, but not under division.
Every prime is an integer, so prime-only statements inherit the integer closure rules.
A prime divided by a different prime is never an integer; a prime divided by itself is 1.
common_mistakes: Treating 'must produce' as 'can produce' and accepting Integer \div Integer because some cases like 6 \div 3 work.
Forgetting that a prime divided by itself is the lone integer case for prime division, and so mis-ruling on (F).

concept.technique_name: multiple-worker rate equation (Work = Individual Rate \times Workers \times Time)

examples.problem_statement: If 45 people built 1/2 of a pyramid in 288 days, how many days did it take 65 people to build the next 1/6 of the pyramid, rounded to the nearest integer, assuming each person works at the same constant rate?

solution.result: \text{the multi-worker form of } W = R \times T
solution.description: Modify the standard Work = Rate \times Time formula for many workers by inserting the number of workers as a factor.

solution.result: \text{an equation in the single unknown } R
solution.description: Plug the first scenario into that formula: half a pyramid of work, 45 workers, 288 days, leaving the individual rate as the only unknown.
Solve that equation for R by dividing, giving the fraction of a pyramid one person builds in one day.

solution.result: \text{an equation in the single unknown } T
solution.description: Put the individual rate just found back into the same work equation, now with the second scenario's 1/6 of a pyramid and 65 workers.
Solve for T by isolating it, which gives the number of days the 65 people needed.
Round that time to the nearest integer as the question demands.

key_reminders: With multiple identical workers, Work = Individual Rate \times Number of Workers \times Time.
Solve for one person's rate from the first scenario before applying it to the second.
Keep the work amounts as fractions of the whole pyramid on both sides of the equation.
common_mistakes: Reusing 1/2 as the second job's work instead of the next 1/6 of the pyramid.
Scaling 288 days by 45/65 alone and ignoring that the amount of work also changed from 1/2 to 1/6.
Treating R = 1/25,920 as a whole-crew rate rather than a single person's rate, then multiplying by 65 a second time.

concept.technique_name: pick numbers for quantitative comparison with absolute values

examples.problem_statement: |x| = |y|, x \ne 0. Quantity A: x + y. Quantity B: 2x. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: \text{two cases: same sign or opposite signs}
solution.description: Unpack the absolute-value condition: equal magnitudes means the two numbers are either equal or opposites, which is the set of cases to test.
Pick the same-sign case first and compute both quantities; they come out equal, which eliminates choices (A) and (B).
Pick the opposite-sign case and compute both quantities; now they differ, which eliminates choice (C).
Confirm the same-sign case algebraically by substituting x for y in Quantity A, which reproduces Quantity B exactly.
Confirm the opposite-sign case algebraically by substituting -x for y; Quantity A collapses to 0 while Quantity B is nonzero because x \ne 0.
Combine the two cases: since the comparison changes depending on the signs, no single relationship holds.

key_reminders: |x| = |y| means y = x or y = -x; both branches must be tested.
In quantitative comparison, two picks that give different relationships already force answer (D).
The condition x \ne 0 is what keeps 0 and 2x from ever being equal in the opposite-sign case.
common_mistakes: Testing only y = x, seeing x + y = 2x, and choosing (C).
Overlooking the negative branch x = -3, y = 3, where Quantity A exceeds Quantity B and the direction flips.
Ignoring x \ne 0 and letting x = y = 0 make the two quantities equal in the opposite-sign case too.
